**What you should be able to do after this meeting.** Turn your central construct into a variable somebody could record. Specify what the design demands of the data. If nothing measures it, write the instrument that would — and say how many observations it needs to be worth fielding.

## Where to read more

[Adams](https://doi.org/10.4135/9788132108498) ch. 5 on sampling and sample size, ch. 8 on survey design, ch. 14 on whether a measure holds up.

## Session A · 2:05–3:15

Constructs and operationalisation. How do you turn 'sustainability', 'financial literacy' or 'market power' into a variable somebody could actually record? What makes that measure defensible, and what does a proxy cost you? Then work backwards from the design to its data requirements. Unit of observation. Level of aggregation. Time frequency, span, coverage. Which comparisons the data has to contain. Can this be done with county data, or does it need individuals? Finally, the short version of what to ask any dataset before trusting it: what is one row, how many are there, what is missing, what changed over time. The full checklist is on the resources page. You put it to work on real data in meeting 12.

## Session B · 3:35–4:30

Every session B opens with a ten-minute team check-in: what you did
since last week, what is stuck, and who is doing what next. Written
down, and handed in with that session's work.

Sometimes nothing measures your construct. Then you make the measurement yourself. Each team gets a real survey item, broken a different way. Leading. Double-barrelled. An unbalanced scale with no way to disagree. A question that assumes you already do the thing. A hypothetical willingness-to-pay that everybody overstates. Name the flaw, rewrite it, and say what an answer to your version would actually let you conclude. Random rotation, room attacks. Then build your own — the instrument your project needs, whether that is survey items, a choice task, or a simple experiment with a treatment and a control. Then work out how many people it needs. The smallest effect you can detect is roughly four sigma over root n. Quadrupling the sample only halves it. So: with the sample you can afford, is the smallest detectable effect still interesting? If not, you have learned that in October rather than March.

Your team's output is submitted before you leave.
